proof_skeleton_nl: Fix an arbitrary coloring f satisfying the theorem hypothesis. Assume for contradiction that both colors appear; choose a red point O and a green point G. Let r=dist(O,G) and choose a smaller radius s=r/4. By L7, the circle centered at G of radius s contains seven distinct points X1,...,X7. L6 says that any five distinct points on that small circle cannot all be green, so among these seven points at most four are green. Therefore at least three of X1,...,X7 are red. But these three distinct red points lie on a circle centered at G, whose color is green, contradicting L1. Hence both colors cannot occur. Therefore the coloring is constant: there exists c in {red,green} such that every point P has color c. This is exactly the theorem statement.

steps.derives: Assume f : R^2 -> {red,green} satisfies the circumcenter-monochromatic property from the theorem hypothesis.
steps.trivial_justification: This is the theorem assumption specialized to an arbitrary coloring f.

steps.derives: To prove the conclusion, it is enough to show that f does not take both colors. Suppose for contradiction that there exist points O,G in R^2 with f(O)=red and f(G)=green.
steps.trivial_justification: If both colors occur, choose one red point O and one green point G. A contradiction from this choice will show that only one color occurs, hence all points have the same color.

steps.derives: Let r = dist(O,G). Then r > 0 because O and G have different colors, so O != G. Define s = r/4. Then 0 < s < r/2.
steps.trivial_justification: Different colors imply O and G are distinct, so dist(O,G)>0. Then s=r/4 satisfies the required inequalities immediately.

steps.derives: There exist seven pairwise distinct points X1,X2,X3,X4,X5,X6,X7 on the circle centered at G with radius s.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L7 to the center G and the positive radius s.

steps.derives: Among the seven points X1,...,X7, at most four are green.
steps.trivial_justification: If at least five of the seven points were green, choose any five green ones. They are pairwise distinct and lie on the circle centered at G with radius s, so L6 would force at least one of them to be red, a contradiction.

steps.derives: Among the seven points X1,...,X7, at least three are red.
steps.trivial_justification: There are seven total points and at most four green points, so at least three must be red.

steps.derives: This is impossible, because G is green and three distinct red points on the circle centered at G with radius s contradict L1.
steps.trivial_justification: The points from A6 are distinct by A4, they all lie on the same circle centered at G by A4, and G is green by A2. L1 says a circle centered at a green point contains at most two red points.

steps.derives: Therefore the assumption that both colors occur is false. Hence there exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: If both colors do not occur, the image of f is a singleton subset of {red,green}. Let c be that unique color. Then every point P has color c.

steps.derives: For every function f : R^2 -> {red,green}, if for all noncollinear points A,B,C with f(A)=f(B)=f(C), the circumcenter of triangle ABC also has that same color, then there exists c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: This restates the result proved for an arbitrary coloring f under the theorem hypothesis.
